newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr storms 6-yr highs on offshore wave.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr storms 6-yr highs on offshore wave.

text.p: The Australian dollar stormed to a two-month high on its U.S. counterpart and no less than a six-year peak on its trade weighted index Wednesday.

Traders said U.S. names led the charge offshore and were reinforced by battalions of bids from Tokyo as long-absent yen/A$ samurai bonds made a return. Flows did turn two-way as Asian selling appeared, but pullbacks were surprisingly brief.
"The demand's coming from all over the place -- U.S. funds, Swiss banks, Tokyo securities houses," said one impressed dealer. "The market's clearly getting bulled-up."
By 5.00 pm (0545 GMT) the local currency had crested at US$0.7941/46, its best close since January 2, having swept to an early US$0.7930/35 from US$0.7875/80 late here Tuesday.

The latest advance meant the dollar had risen by more than five percent since it troughed at US$0.7550 on February 12 and added yet another technical scalp to its collection with the capture of US$0.7910, the ceiling for the last week.

It also brought bulls to within spitting distance of a key chart goal at US$0.7960, a level which derives its technical importance from being a 62 percent retracement of the fall from the six-year high of US$0.8212 in December to the US$0.7550 low.
Analysts expected this barrier to be a tough one, but felt it would a great attractor to chart followers and momentum funds and could be reached as early as tonight.
Once there, a pause for consolidation was likely before the dollar could tackle the psychologically charged territory above 80 cents, they added.
The currency's strength was far from limited to the U.S. dollar as offshore funds dumped low yielders like the yen, marks and Swiss francs for the more ample returns of A$ assets.
The local dollar shot to a fresh 4-1/2 year high on the yen at 97.45/55, a rise of almost two yen from Tuesday's 95.55/65.
Traders reported heavy buying out of Tokyo and rumours of a yen/A$ dual currency samurai issue proved well founded when Nomura launched a 30 billion yen bond for a German bank.
This followed a reverse yen/A$ issue Tuesday -- which pays the coupon in dollars as opposed to the principal -- and was the first of the type since early January.

These were a huge hit with yield-strapped Japanese investors last year, but demand dried up when domestic rates were cut for the third time in December. Recently, however, the risk of an easing had been replaced by talk of steady rates and even a tightening by year-end, and market yields had risen accordingly.

The spread on two-year Australian bonds over their U.S. counterpart, for instance, had yawned to 65 basis points from less than 40 a few weeks ago while December 90-day bank bill futures were pricing in a 75 basis point rise in the present 6.00 percent official cash rate.
Australian 10-year bonds actually offered the highest yield of the whole OECD even though inflation here was expected to remain around a historically low 2.0 percent all this year.
Such lofty real returns dwarfed those available in Europe and helped lift the dollar to five year highs on both the mark and Swiss franc and a six year peak in trade weighted terms.

On this index, which measures the A$ against a basket of currencies weighted to reflect the importance of Australia's trade, the dollar climbed 0.5 point to 61.0, its first visit here since October 1990.
Today's domestic data supported the outlook for steady rates with the Westpac consumer confidence index rising 4.9 percent in March after a shock 7.9 percent drop in February.
The market now awaits Thursday's key labour data for February and housing finance commitments for January in the expectation they will continue the run of upbeat indicators.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
